read.title: No gaps, no jumps
text: Informally, a function is continuous if you can draw its graph without lifting your pencil. The precise version checks three things at a point a: f(a) must exist, the limit as x approaches a must exist, and those two numbers must be equal. Each kind of failure has a name. A removable discontinuity is a single hole, where the limit exists but the function value is missing or misplaced. A jump discontinuity has left and right limits that disagree. An infinite discontinuity sits at a vertical asymptote.

Continuity pays off in the Intermediate Value Theorem. If f is continuous on [a, b], it cannot skip any value between f(a) and f(b). So if f(1) is negative and f(2) is positive, the graph must cross zero somewhere in between. This is the guarantee behind root-finding by repeated halving.

Limits at infinity describe long-run behavior. For a rational function, only the highest powers matter for large x. If the top and bottom have the same degree, the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients, which gives a horizontal asymptote. If the bottom's degree is larger, the limit is 0. If the top's degree is larger, there is no horizontal asymptote at all.
